title: Delayed post-hypoxic leukoencephalopathy following alcohol consumption and cardiopulmonary arrest
case_prompt:
A 43-year-old man with no significant medical history was found unconscious outdoors after an evening of heavy alcohol consumption. Emergency Medical Services performed CPR and intubated him on scene because of decreased respiratory effort and a low Glasgow Coma Scale score. On arrival at the hospital he remained mechanically ventilated, unresponsive, and hemodynamically stable.

Initial noncontrast head CT showed no acute intracranial abnormality. Echocardiography was unremarkable. Lumbar puncture revealed normal cell counts without xanthochromia. Electroencephalography demonstrated paroxysmal epileptiform activity, and repeat studies documented ongoing epileptiform discharges despite anticonvulsant therapy.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain on hospital day 1, including T2, FLAIR, diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) sequences, showed no abnormalities.

Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, electrolytes (sodium 144 mmol/L), renal function, and C-reactive protein level, were noncontributory. Arterial lactate was 1.7 mmol/L and pH was 7.35. Liver tests were mildly elevated (ALT 153 IU/L, AST 122 IU/L, GGT 305 IU/L). Viral hepatitis serologies were negative. Troponin was 0.31 μg/mL without ECG evidence of myocardial infarction. Toxicology screening revealed a blood alcohol level of 48.8 mmol/L and benzodiazepines; opiates and amphetamines were negative.

On hospital day 6, repeat MRI of the brain demonstrated new areas of increased signal on DWI with corresponding low signal on ADC mapping, symmetrically involving the white matter of the centrum semiovale and posterior parietal regions. Conventional T2 and FLAIR sequences remained normal.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Acute anoxic brain injury was considered because of the cardiac arrest and delayed resuscitation — “Clinically, he was suspected to have an underlying anoxic brain injury given the delayed resuscitation efforts, although normal initial imaging was unusual.”  
2. Osmotic demyelination syndrome was included in the differential — “Differential diagnoses included … osmotic demyelination syndrome …”  
3. Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome was included in the differential — “Differential diagnoses included … posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome …”  
4. Delayed post hypoxic leukoencephalopathy was favored because of the delayed onset of white matter changes on DWI despite normal T2/FLAIR scans — “DPHL was the final diagnosis given to our patient since it was most consistent with the delayed onset MRI changes and white matter involvement.” “The fact that the white matter changes were only seen on DWI sequence suggests that the changes were picked up early and not yet apparent on standard T2 and FLAIR sequences.”
